title: Trees and Graphs Revision Notes: Binary Trees, BSTs, Heaps, Tries, BFS, DFS, Dijkstra and Union-Find
summary: Night-before revision notes on tree structures (binary trees, BSTs, heaps, tries) and graph algorithms (representations, BFS, DFS, topological sort, Dijkstra, union-find). Each chapter covers the model, the mechanism, comparisons, a worked example and the usual mistakes.

chapters.title: Binary Trees, BSTs and Traversals
points: Definition: a binary tree node has at most 2 children; height h is the longest root-to-leaf path, and a BST adds the invariant left subtree < node < right subtree for every node, not just the direct children.

Mechanism: BST search, insert and delete walk one root-to-leaf path, so each costs O(h). That is O(log n) when balanced and O(n) when skewed. Deleting a node with two children replaces it with its inorder successor.

Comparison: preorder is node-left-right (copy a tree), inorder is left-node-right (gives sorted order in a BST), postorder is left-right-node (delete a tree, compute heights). Level-order uses a queue.
Example: recursive inorder is def inorder(n): if n: inorder(n.left); visit(n); inorder(n.right). Inorder of 2-1-3 with root 2 gives 1,2,3.

Mistakes: validating a BST by comparing only a node with its children (pass min/max bounds down instead), inserting sorted data into an unbalanced BST (it becomes a linked list), and hitting recursion depth limits on skewed trees.

chapters.title: Heaps and Tries
points: Definition: a binary heap is a complete binary tree where each parent is <= its children (min-heap) or >= (max-heap), stored in an array with children at 2i+1 and 2i+2 and parent at (i-1)//2.
Mechanism: push appends the item and sifts up in O(log n); pop swaps the root with the last item and sifts down in O(log n); peek is O(1); building a heap from n items with heapify is O(n).

Comparison: a heap gives the min or max quickly but is not sorted and cannot search efficiently (O(n)), while a BST gives ordered search in O(h) (O(log n) if balanced, O(n) if skewed) but no O(1) min peek. A trie lookup costs O(L) in key length, independent of the number of keys.

Example: top-k largest uses a min-heap of size k: push each item, pop when size exceeds k, O(n log k). A trie node holds children[char] and an is_end flag; insert and search walk one character per step.

Mistakes: forgetting that Python's heapq is only a min-heap (push negated values for a max-heap), treating the heap array as sorted, and omitting is_end so that 'app' wrongly matches when only 'apple' was inserted. Tries also cost a lot of memory.

chapters.title: Graph Representations, BFS and DFS
points: Definition: a graph is vertices V plus edges E, directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted. An adjacency list takes O(V+E) space; an adjacency matrix takes O(V^2).
Comparison: use a list for sparse graphs (iterate neighbours in O(deg)); use a matrix for dense graphs or when you need an O(1) edge-exists check.

Mechanism: BFS uses a queue and a visited set, expands level by level, and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs in O(V+E). DFS uses recursion or an explicit stack, goes deep first, and runs in O(V+E).

Example: BFS skeleton is q=deque([s]); seen={s}; while q: u=q.popleft(); for v in adj[u]: if v not in seen: seen.add(v); q.append(v). Use DFS for cycle detection, connected components and path existence.

Mistakes: marking visited on pop instead of on push (duplicates enter the queue), forgetting visited on cyclic graphs (infinite loop), looping only from one start node and missing disconnected components, and using BFS distances on weighted graphs.

chapters.title: Topological Sort and Dijkstra
points: Definition: a topological sort is a linear order of a DAG's vertices where every edge u->v puts u before v. It exists only if there is no cycle. Dijkstra finds single-source shortest paths with non-negative edge weights.

Mechanism: Kahn's algorithm computes indegrees, queues the nodes with indegree 0, pops one, decrements its neighbours' indegrees, and queues any that reach 0, in O(V+E). If fewer than V nodes are output, the graph has a cycle.
Mechanism: Dijkstra keeps a min-heap of (dist,node), pops the smallest, skips it if the popped dist is stale, and relaxes each edge with dist[v]=min(dist[v],dist[u]+w). It runs in O((V+E) log V).
Example: course prerequisites A->B->C gives order A,B,C. For Dijkstra on A-(1)->B-(2)->C and A-(5)->C, dist[C] is 3, not 5.

Mistakes: running Dijkstra with negative edges (use Bellman-Ford instead), forgetting the stale-entry check when using a heap with lazy deletion, and expecting a topological sort of a cyclic graph. DFS-based topological sort outputs reverse postorder.

chapters.title: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union)
points: Definition: union-find tracks disjoint sets with a parent array, where parent[x]==x marks a root; find(x) returns the set's root and union(a,b) merges two sets.

Mechanism: path compression sets parent[x]=find(parent[x]) during find, and union by rank or size attaches the smaller tree under the larger. Together they give amortized O(alpha(n)), effectively constant time.
Comparison: use union-find for dynamic connectivity and merging, where it is faster than rerunning BFS or DFS after each added edge. It cannot split sets or delete edges.
Example: Kruskal's MST sorts edges by weight and adds an edge only if find(u)!=find(v), then calls union. A union that finds equal roots means the edge would form a cycle.

Mistakes: calling union on the raw nodes instead of on their find() roots, skipping both path compression and union by rank or size (find degrades to O(n); union by rank alone still gives O(log n)), and initialising parent[i] to something other than i.

chapters.title: Trees and Graphs Cheat Sheet
points: Complexities: BST ops are O(h), with h = log n balanced and n skewed. Heap push/pop is O(log n), peek is O(1) and heapify is O(n). Trie ops are O(L). BFS/DFS and Kahn's are O(V+E). Dijkstra is O((V+E) log V). Union-find is O(alpha(n)).
Traversal picks: inorder gives sorted BST output, preorder copies a tree, postorder deletes a tree, level-order uses a queue.
Structure picks: use a heap for top-k and a priority queue, a trie for prefix search, an adjacency list for sparse graphs and a matrix for dense graphs.
Algorithm picks: BFS for unweighted shortest paths, Dijkstra for non-negative weights, Kahn's or DFS for DAG ordering, union-find for connectivity and Kruskal.
Pre-submit checks: BST bounds passed down, visited marked on push, disconnected components covered, no negative edges for Dijkstra, cycle check on topological sort, union applied to roots.
